title: What are memory-mapped files (`FileChannel.map` → `MappedByteBuffer`), how do they map a file region into memory for OS-paged, zero-copy access, and when are they useful (very large files, high-throughput I/O, inter-process shared memory)?
shortTitle: What are memory-mapped files, how do they work, and when are they useful?

s1_definition.profdef: A memory-mapped file maps a region of a file directly into the process's virtual address space, so that reading and writing the file becomes reading and writing memory. In Java you obtain one by calling `FileChannel.map(mode, position, size)`, which returns a `MappedByteBuffer`. The operating system loads file pages into memory on demand (demand paging) and writes dirty pages back to disk lazily, so there is no explicit read or write system call per access and no copy between a kernel buffer and a user buffer — this is the zero-copy, OS-paged benefit. Memory-mapped files are useful for very large files, high-throughput I/O, and sharing memory between processes.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a giant archive book of every transaction, far too big to photocopy and carry around. Normal file reading is like asking a clerk to fetch and photocopy one page at a time whenever you want it (a system call plus a copy each time). A memory-mapped file is like the bank magically placing the entire archive book on your desk, but only materializing each page the moment you actually turn to it. You read and write pages as if they were right in front of you, and the bank quietly syncs any pages you wrote back into the master archive in the background. Two clerks can even be given the same magic book, so when one writes on a page the other immediately sees it — that is shared memory between processes.
s1_definition.oneliner: A memory-mapped file maps a file region into memory via FileChannel.map, giving a MappedByteBuffer where the OS pages data in on demand and writes it back lazily, enabling zero-copy, large-file, and shared-memory access.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A memory-mapped file maps a region of a file directly into the process's virtual address space, so that reading and writing the file becomes reading and writing memory. In Java you obtain one by calling `FileChannel.map(mode, position, size)`, which returns a `MappedByteBuffer`. The operating system loads file pages into memory on demand (demand paging) and writes dirty pages back to disk lazily, so there is no explicit read or write system call per access and no copy between a kernel buffer and a user buffer — this is the zero-copy, OS-paged benefit. Memory-mapped files are useful for very large files, high-throughput I/O, and sharing memory between processes.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has a giant archive book of every transaction, far too big to photocopy and carry around. Normal file reading is like asking a clerk to fetch and photocopy one page at a time whenever you want it (a system call plus a copy each time). A memory-mapped file is like the bank magically placing the entire archive book on your desk, but only materializing each page the moment you actually turn to it. You read and write pages as if they were right in front of you, and the bank quietly syncs any pages you wrote back into the master archive in the background. Two clerks can even be given the same magic book, so when one writes on a page the other immediately sees it — that is shared memory between processes.

**One line to remember:** A memory-mapped file maps a file region into memory via FileChannel.map, giving a MappedByteBuffer where the OS pages data in on demand and writes it back lazily, enabling zero-copy, large-file, and shared-memory access.

sections.s2_technical:
Normal file I/O goes through system calls. Each `read` copies bytes from the OS page cache into a buffer you supply, and each `write` copies the other way. For large files or high request rates, these system calls and copies add up. Memory mapping removes the per-access system call and the copy: the file's pages are mapped into your virtual address space, and the hardware memory-management unit, together with the OS, handles bringing pages in and out.

The mechanism is demand paging. When you call `FileChannel.map`, the OS does not read the whole file; it sets up page-table entries that point at the file. The first time you touch a byte in a page, the CPU raises a page fault, the OS reads just that page from disk into physical memory, and your access continues. Pages you never touch are never loaded. When you write to a mapped region in read-write mode, the page becomes dirty, and the OS writes it back to disk later, either when memory pressure evicts it or when you explicitly call `force()` to flush. This lazy write-back is why mapped I/O is fast but also why durability needs care.

In Java the API is `FileChannel.map(FileChannel.MapMode mode, long position, long size)`. The modes are `READ_ONLY`, `READ_WRITE`, and `PRIVATE`. `READ_ONLY` maps the file for reading and throws if you try to write. `READ_WRITE` lets your writes propagate back to the file and, if the mapping is shared, to other processes mapping the same file. `PRIVATE` gives copy-on-write semantics: your writes are visible only to you and are never written back to the file. The returned `MappedByteBuffer` is a `ByteBuffer` whose storage is the mapped region; you use the usual `get`, `put`, `getLong`, `putInt`, and positional variants.

A key limitation is that the `size` argument is an `int`-bounded `long` in practice up to about two gigabytes per mapping, because `ByteBuffer` indexes with `int`. For files larger than that you create multiple mappings over different regions, or use the newer Foreign Function and Memory API, which can map a whole large file as one `MemorySegment` via `FileChannel.map(mode, offset, size, arena)` without the two-gigabyte ceiling and with deterministic unmapping when the arena closes.

Durability and flushing matter in banking. Because write-back is lazy, data you wrote to a `MappedByteBuffer` may still be only in memory, not on disk, after your code moves on. Calling `mappedBuffer.force()` asks the OS to flush dirty pages to disk, which you must do before you can claim the data is durably persisted, for example after writing a committed ledger record.

Unmapping is a notorious wrinkle. There is no public `unmap` method on the old `MappedByteBuffer`; the mapping is released only when the buffer is garbage-collected and its cleaner runs, which is non-deterministic. This means a mapped file can stay locked or its disk space pinned longer than expected, and on Windows you sometimes cannot delete the file until the mapping is released. The Foreign Function and Memory API solves this cleanly because closing the arena unmaps immediately.

When is memory mapping the right tool? First, very large files you access randomly, such as a database file, an index, or a large log, where loading the whole file would blow memory but random page access is natural. Second, high-throughput I/O where avoiding per-read system calls and copies is worth it, which is why Kafka, Lucene, and many databases map their segment files. Third, inter-process shared memory: two processes mapping the same file in shared read-write mode see each other's writes through the same physical pages, giving a fast IPC channel without sockets. The trade-offs are that mapping is backed by the OS page cache so it competes with other memory users, write durability needs explicit `force`, unmapping is non-deterministic with the old API, and a disk I/O error during a page fault surfaces as a hard-to-handle error rather than a clean `IOException` at a specific call.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India keeps a large end-of-day ledger file with fixed-size records, one per account, holding the account balance in paise. Reporting jobs need to read and occasionally update individual balances by position, but the file is far too large to load entirely into memory. This is exactly the memory-mapped case: map the file so each record access touches only the page that record lives on, with no full load and no per-access system call.

Problem 2 — A settlement update must change Rajesh's balance in place, and the change must be durable before we report success. This is the write-back and force case: we write to the `MappedByteBuffer` and then call `force()` to flush the dirty page to disk so the update survives a crash.

Problem 3 — A developer mapped the file, updated it, and then tried to delete it, but the delete failed on some platforms because the mapping was still held. This is the non-deterministic unmap risk: with the old API you cannot force an unmap, so we use the Foreign Function and Memory API arena so the mapping is released deterministically when we close it.

The mini-project maps a fixed-size-record ledger file, reads Rajesh's and Priya's balances by index, updates Rajesh's balance with a durable `force`, and reads it back. Each record is eight bytes, a long of paise.

The code contains: a `MappedLedger` using FileChannel.map and MappedByteBuffer; and a runnable demo that creates the file, reads, updates with force, and re-reads.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two account balances to persist in a mapped ledger: Rajesh Rs.1000000 at index 0 and Priya Rs.250000 at index 1, followed by a Rs.50000 debit to Rajesh.

Step 1: A temp file is created and opened as a `FileChannel`. `channel.map(READ_WRITE, 0, 16, arena)` maps the 16-byte file into memory. The OS sets up page-table entries but does not necessarily read anything yet.

Step 2: `setBalance(0, Rs.1000000)` converts to 100000000 paise and writes that long at mapped index 0. The first touch of that page triggers a page fault, the OS brings the page in, and the write marks the page dirty. `setBalance(1, Rs.250000)` writes 25000000 at index 1.

Step 3: `flush()` calls `channel.force(true)`, which writes the dirty pages to disk. Now the data is durable — it would survive a crash.

Step 4: `getBalance(0)` reads the long back from the mapped page, 100000000 paise, and rebuilds Rs.1000000.00. No system call, no copy — just a memory read from a page already resident.

Step 5: The settlement debit computes Rs.950000, `setBalance(0, Rs.950000)` writes 95000000, and `flush()` makes it durable.

Step 6: `getBalance(0)` now returns Rs.950000.00.

Step 7: `close()` closes the arena, which unmaps the region deterministically, then closes the channel. Because the mapping is released, `Files.deleteIfExists` succeeds on every platform.

```
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:40 PM com.bank.ledger.MappedLedgerDemo main
INFO: Mapped read Rajesh: Rs.1000000.00
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:40 PM com.bank.ledger.MappedLedgerDemo main
INFO: Mapped read Priya : Rs.250000.00
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:40 PM com.bank.ledger.MappedLedgerDemo main
INFO: After Rs.50000 debit, Rajesh: Rs.950000.00
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:40 PM com.bank.ledger.MappedLedgerDemo main
INFO: Ledger unmapped and temp file deleted
```

```
  Input: idx0=Rajesh Rs.1,000,000  idx1=Priya Rs.250,000  then debit 50,000
    │
    ▼
  FileChannel.open(ledger.dat, READ/WRITE/CREATE)
    │
    ▼
  channel.map(READ_WRITE, 0, 16, arena) → MemorySegment (file mapped into memory)
    │  (OS sets page tables; pages loaded on first touch = demand paging)
    ▼
  setBalance(0, 1,000,000) → write 100,000,000 @ idx0   (page fault → dirty page)
  setBalance(1,   250,000) → write  25,000,000 @ idx1
    │
    ▼
  flush() → channel.force(true)   ─── dirty pages → DISK (durable)
    │
    ▼
  getBalance(0) → read 100,000,000 → Rs.1,000,000.00   (pure memory read, zero-copy)
    │
    ▼
  debit: setBalance(0, 950,000) → flush() → DISK
    │
    ▼
  close(): arena.close() → DETERMINISTIC UNMAP → channel.close()
    │
    ▼
  Files.delete(ledger.dat)  (mapping released, delete safe on all OS)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A memory-mapped file maps a region of a file directly into the process's virtual address space, so that reading and writing the file becomes reading and writing memory. In Java I call FileChannel dot map with a mode, a position, and a size, and I get back a MappedByteBuffer, or with the newer Foreign Function and Memory API a memory segment. The operating system uses demand paging, meaning it loads a file page into memory only the first time I touch it, and it writes dirty pages back to disk lazily. That removes the per-access system call and the copy between a kernel buffer and a user buffer, which is the zero-copy benefit, and it lets me work with files far larger than I could ever load fully into memory.

I use memory mapping in three situations. First, very large files I access randomly, such as a ledger, an index, or a database segment, where mapping lets each access touch only the relevant page. Second, high-throughput I/O, which is why systems like Kafka and Lucene map their segment files to avoid per-read system calls. Third, inter-process shared memory, because two processes mapping the same file in shared read-write mode see each other's writes through the same physical pages, giving a fast communication channel without sockets.

In my banking work at National Bank of India I used this for an end-of-day ledger file of fixed-size records, one balance per account in paise. Reporting and settlement jobs read and updated balances by position without ever loading the whole file. The two things I am always careful about are durability and unmapping. Because write-back is lazy, after writing a committed record I call force to flush the dirty pages to disk before I report success, otherwise a crash could lose data that was only in memory. And the classic MappedByteBuffer has no public unmap method, so the mapping is released only when the buffer is garbage-collected, which is non-deterministic and on some platforms even blocks deleting the file. I solve that by mapping through an arena in the Foreign Function and Memory API, because closing the arena unmaps the region immediately and deterministically. The size limit of about two gigabytes per MappedByteBuffer is another reason I prefer the memory segment API for very large files, since it maps the whole file as one segment without that ceiling.
